findings.text: Someone opening the Athena site expects to learn what Athena is, but the page is entirely about a different project, firstmate. Athena is never named or explained, so the newcomer cannot say what the site is.
findings.source: <title>How firstmate handles work</title>; footer: "Generated from studies/firstmate-work-handling"

findings.text: The opening line assumes the reader already knows what firstmate is and what a "study" is. Neither is introduced, and nothing says who made the study or why.
findings.source: "A reading of firstmate at one pinned commit, from the study firstmate-work-handling."

findings.text: This is the closest the page comes to a definition. It doesn't say the workers are AI coding agents or who would use firstmate, so the reader still can't tell what problem it solves or why it matters.
findings.source: What firstmate is: "Firstmate takes an item from a backlog and gives it to a worker, which does the work in its own isolated worktree"

findings.text: There is no clear next step: the repository URL and every source are plain text, not links, and nothing says how to install, try, or learn more about firstmate or Athena.
findings.source: Pinned firstmate commit: "https://github.com/kunchenguid/firstmate.git"; claim sources such as "AGENTS.md:206-206"

findings.text: The 'Start here' section does well: it explains the page's own layout, walks one task from start to finish in order, and lists the failure cases. A newcomer who already knows the context could follow the task lifecycle.
The glossary is near the top and is long and detailed. That makes the page feel like reference material, and some terms are still left vague, such as "The text says no more about who the captain is."
This note is about the tool that generated the page and uses its internal field name (guard_evaluated_by). A newcomer cannot make sense of it.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f2: "A guard of none has no value in guard_evaluated_by for nobody. These transitions carry agent there as a placeholder"

findings.text: Every statement is backed by a claim with file-and-line sources, which is trustworthy, but the citations break up the text. The sources point to lines in the firstmate repository that the reader cannot open from the page.
findings.source: Each statement ends with bracketed claim links such as "[c1] [c22]"
